title: Building an Agentic Desktop on Fedora 44: Inspired by Omarchy
text:
# Building an Agentic Desktop on Fedora 44: Inspired by Omarchy

Most Linux "rice" showcases focus purely on aesthetic vanity: an anime wallpaper, a transparent terminal, and an MPD visualizer dancing to synthwave. But when your workstation is your command center for developing production software and coordinating autonomous AI agents, aesthetics cannot come at the expense of stability, system isolation, or responsiveness.

I have spent the past several days architecting a daily-driver desktop environment on **Fedora 44**. The visual inspiration and ergonomics draw heavily from [Omarchy](https://github.com/omarchy)—the hyper-minimalist, keyboard-driven desktop concept—but the underlying infrastructure is tailored specifically for bleeding-edge software engineering and AI-assisted workflows.

Here is the process of how I stripped away desktop bloat, solved stubborn Wayland integration bugs on bleeding-edge Fedora 44, and built an "Agentic Desktop" that acts as a first-class pair programmer.

---

## 1. Architectural Foundation: Why Fedora 44 over Arch?

Omarchy traditionally lives on Arch Linux, where rolling releases make package discovery trivial. However, for a production DevOps and AI workstation running containerized clusters, enforced security policies, and custom kernel modules, Fedora 44 provides distinct advantages:

1. **Enterprise Plumber Foundations**: Modern systemd user service management, native SELinux enforcement, and `dnf5` for rapid, deterministic package resolution.
2. **Bleeding-Edge Kernel & Wayland**: Fedora tracks upstream kernel versions closely, giving us first-class AMD/Intel GPU driver support for Hyprland compositing without Arch's occasional ABI mismatch surprises.
3. **Zero GNOME Bleed**: I have grown to appreciate GNOME, but it lacks the razor-sharp fluidity of Hyprland. Rather than running a hybrid desktop where GNOME Shell processes linger in the background consuming resources, I decoupled the entire graphical stack. Display management hands off directly to Hyprland, with zero GNOME daemons holding D-Bus locks.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Core ["Compositor & Display Layer"]
        SDDM["Display Manager / SDDM"] --> Hyprland["Hyprland Wayland Compositor"]
    end

    subgraph Shell ["Shell & Telemetry Interface"]
        Hyprland --> Waybar["Waybar (cybrcore powerline)"]
        Hyprland --> SwayNC["SwayNC Notification Center"]
        Hyprland --> Fuzzel["Fuzzel App & Power Launcher"]
    end

    subgraph Agentic ["Agentic AI Workstation Integration"]
        Waybar --> AgentWidget["Agent Telemetry (agent.sh)"]
        Hyprland --> AgentScratch["Scratchpad Workspace (Super+A)"]
        AgentCore["Antigravity / Butler Engine"] --> WinstonSay["Voice Feedback (~/.local/bin/winston-say)"]
        AgentCore --> AgentWidget
    end
```

---

## 2. Decoupling the Desktop Stack

Building a standalone Wayland workstation means assembling purpose-built modular utilities rather than relying on a heavy desktop environment.

### The Component Matrix

| Function | Package / Utility | Keybinding | Rationale |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Compositor** | `hyprland` | Native | Smooth tiling, dynamic workspaces, low-latency rendering. |
| **Status Bar** | `waybar` | Auto-start | Powerline chevron aesthetics with custom telemetry modules. |
| **Notification Center**| `swaynotificationcenter` | `Super + N` | Notification panel with Do-Not-Disturb and quick action toggles. |
| **Application Launcher**| `fuzzel` | `Super + Space` | Wayland-native, instant fuzzy search with hex palette matching. |
| **Power Menu** | `fuzzel-power` | `Super + Escape` | Clean script for Lock, Suspend, Reboot, and Shutdown. |
| **File Management** | `yazi` / `thunar` | `Super + Shift + E` | CLI velocity with Yazi; GTK file picker fallback with Thunar. |
| **Screen Capture** | `omarchy-capture` | `Print` / `Super + Print` | Screen area clipping, full screenshot, OCR, and MP4 screen recording. |
| **Hotkey Cheatsheet** | `omarchy-hotkeys` | `Super + K` | Dynamic Fuzzel-driven popup documenting all active keybindings. |

---

## 3. Designing for the Agentic Era

What makes an operating system "agentic"? It is not simply opening a browser tab to an LLM chat window. An agentic desktop treats AI processes as first-class background workers with dedicated system telemetry, hotkey scratchpads, and hands-free feedback loops.

### A. The Agent Telemetry Bar Module
In `~/.config/waybar/scripts/agent.sh`, a lightweight daemon polls active agent sockets and process flags:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# agent.sh - Telemetry widget for Antigravity & Claude processes

STATE_FILE="/tmp/agent_state"

if [ -f "$STATE_FILE" ]; then
    STATE=$(cat "$STATE_FILE")
    case "$STATE" in
        "active")
            echo '{"text": "󰚩 AGY", "class": "running", "tooltip": "Antigravity Agent: Executing Task"}'
            ;;
        "review")
            echo '{"text": "󰚩 Review", "class": "review", "tooltip": "Antigravity Agent: Waiting for Approval"}'
            ;;
        *)
            echo '{"text": "󰚩 Idle", "class": "idle", "tooltip": "Antigravity: Standby"}'
            ;;
    esac
else
    echo '{"text": "󰚩 Ready", "class": "standby", "tooltip": "No active tasks running"}'
fi
```

This updates our Waybar tray cleanly with custom Nerd Font icons (`󰚩 AGY`), styled to pulsate gently in gold or cyan when an agent is compiling or refactoring files.

### B. Instant-Access Agent Scratchpad
In `~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf`, I mapped a dedicated dropdown terminal scratchpad bound to `Super + A`:

```ini
# Special workspace for Agent CLI
workspace = special:agent, gapsout:40, gapsin:10
bind = $mainMod, A, togglespecialworkspace, agent
bind = $mainMod, A, exec, hyprctl dispatch submap reset
```

Hitting `Super + A` drops an accelerated Kitty terminal hosting our running agent session directly over the current workspace, allowing instant pair-programming prompts without disturbing code layouts.

### C. Voice Telemetry: Winston Butler Protocol
When agents perform background compilations, multi-file edits, or test suites, switching focus to read CLI logs introduces unnecessary context switching (as parsing verbose terminal output amidst deep focus breaks flow). I implemented `winston-say`:

```bash
~/.local/bin/winston-say "Unit tests passed cleanly across all 14 test suites, sir."
```

Using local high-fidelity speech synthesis, the desktop audibly announces completed workflows, test results, or prompt completions in an understated British butler cadence.

---

## 4. Hard-Earned Debugging Lessons: Real Wayland Pitfalls

Building on Wayland outside of a monolithic desktop environment requires solving edge-case protocol quirks. Here are four issues encountered and how I fixed them.

### Bug 1: The Squeezed 493px GTK Save Dialog
**Symptom**: Whenever an application (VSCode, Thunar, or a browser) opened a file chooser or "Save As" portal dialog, Hyprland treated it as a regular tiled window. On an ultrawide monitor, the file dialog was squashed into an unreadable vertical sliver measuring 493px wide.

**Root Cause**: The FreeDesktop file chooser portal (`xdg-desktop-portal-gtk`) does not declare a default window geometry when launched inside a standalone compositor without GNOME Shell managing modal hints.

**The Fix**: Explicit window rules in `~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf`:

```ini
# Force modal dialogs and file pickers to float and center at usable dimensions
windowrulev2 = float, class:^(xdg-desktop-portal-gtk)$
windowrulev2 = center, class:^(xdg-desktop-portal-gtk)$
windowrulev2 = size 75% 75%, class:^(xdg-desktop-portal-gtk)$

windowrulev2 = float, title:^(Open File|Save File|All Files|Select a Folder)$
windowrulev2 = center, title:^(Open File|Save File|All Files|Select a Folder)$
windowrulev2 = size 75% 75%, title:^(Open File|Save File|All Files|Select a Folder)$
```

### Bug 2: The Waybar `hyprland/window` Syntax Trap
**Symptom**: Attempting to display the application icon alongside the active window title caused Waybar to crash or fail to parse the configuration:
```json
"hyprland/window": {
    "format": "{icon} {title}", // ERROR: Unknown format argument
    "max-length": 40
}
```

**Root Cause**: Unlike the `sway/window` module, Waybar's `hyprland/window` module does not implement an `{icon}` token in the format string. Icons must be enabled via a boolean property:

```json
"hyprland/window": {
    "format": "{title}",
    "icon": true,
    "icon-size": 16,
    "max-length": 40
}
```

Ultimately, to keep Waybar visually clean and prevent distraction while coding, we removed the module entirely in favor of an animated media marquee and our agent telemetry monitor.

### Bug 3: UTF-8 Marquee Slicing in `mediaplayer.py`
**Symptom**: When playing tracks with multibyte characters (emojis or Japanese kanji), our Waybar media scroller threw intermittent `UnicodeDecodeError` exceptions or stuttered violently.

**Root Cause**: Slicing strings using naive byte offsets in Python can cut a multi-byte UTF-8 character in half.

**The Fix**: A robust GLib timer loop operating strictly on Python string code points:

```python
def update_marquee(self):
    if len(self.full_title) <= self.max_len:
        self.displayed_text = self.full_title
    else:
        # Proper character slicing with wraparound padding
        padded = self.full_title + "   |   "
        self.displayed_text = (padded[self.offset:] + padded[:self.offset])[:self.max_len]
        self.offset = (self.offset + 1) % len(padded)
    
    self.write_output()
    return True # Keep GLib.timeout_add running every 300ms
```

### Bug 4: The D-Bus Notification Center Collision
**Symptom**: After configuring `SwayNotificationCenter` (`swaync`) for notifications, the daemon refused to launch on boot, erroring with:
`Failed to acquire org.freedesktop.Notifications: Name already registered`.

**Root Cause**: Fedora's default packaging had pulled in `dunst.service` via a dependency, and the systemd user bus was activating Dunst before SwayNC could claim the bus name.

**The Fix**: Masking the competing service permanently at the user level:

```bash
systemctl --user stop dunst.service
systemctl --user mask dunst.service
systemctl --user enable --now swaync.service
```

Now, notifications display in clean top-center cyber banners with action buttons, fully accessible via `Super + N`.

---

## 5. Zero-Flicker Dynamic Theming

In many ricing setups, switching a color theme requires restarting the compositor or enduring jarring screen flashes. I engineered a zero-downtime theme switcher (`~/.local/bin/theme-switcher`) supporting 8 distinct palettes (heavily inspired by DHH's Omarchy palette philosophy, yet adapted natively for Waybar and Hyprland IPC):

- **Night City Gold** (`#F2D230`)
- **Cyberpunk Cyan** (`#00F0FF`)
- **Neon Violet** (`#BD93F9`)
- **Matrix Emerald** (`#50FA7B`)
- **Deep Cobalt** (`#0080FF`)
- **Crimson Protocol** (`#FF5555`)
- **Tokyo Night** (`#7AA2F7`)
- **Catppuccin Mocha** (`#CBA6F7`)

### How the Hot-Reload Engine Works
When `Super + Alt + T` triggers a theme swap:
1. **CSS Compilation**: Generates `~/.config/waybar/current_theme.css` with active primary and secondary hex variables.
2. **SVG Recoloring**: Automatically transforms the Powerline chevron SVGs (`re0-left.svg` and `re0-right.svg`) using XML DOM color replacement.
3. **Waybar Signal Reload**: Sends `killall -SIGUSR2 waybar`. Waybar re-reads its stylesheet without restarting its process tree or dropping audio state.
4. **Compositor Border Sync**: Dispatches `hyprctl keyword general:col.active_border "rgba(${COLOR}ee)"` in real time.
5. **Notification Styling**: Writes matching CSS variables to `~/.config/swaync/style.css` and calls `swaync-client -R` to reload styling on the fly.
6. **Wallpaper Crossfade**: Updates the wallpaper backdrop using `swww` or `hyprpaper` from `~/.config/hypr/wallpapers/<theme>/`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor User
    participant Switcher as theme-switcher
    participant Waybar as Waybar
    participant Hyprland as Hyprland Engine
    participant SwayNC as SwayNotificationCenter
    participant SWWW as Wallpaper Daemon

    User->>Switcher: Super + Alt + T (Select Theme)
    Switcher->>Switcher: Write current_theme.css & recolor chevrons
    Switcher->>Waybar: killall -SIGUSR2 waybar
    Waybar-->>User: Seamless instant bar recolor
    Switcher->>Hyprland: hyprctl keyword general:col.active_border
    Hyprland-->>User: Window borders shift immediately
    Switcher->>SwayNC: swaync-client -R
    Switcher->>SWWW: Transition wallpaper image
```

---

## 6. Daily Workflow & Keybinding Philosophy

The keybindings prioritize ergonomic efficiency, grouping operational modes logically—which I unashamedly adapted from DHH's key config for Omarchy:

```
Navigation & Window Management
├── Super + [1-9]           : Instant Workspace Switch
├── Super + Shift + [1-9]   : Move Active Window to Workspace
├── Super + Q               : Close Active Window
├── Super + F               : Toggle Fullscreen
└── Super + V               : Toggle Floating

System & App Launchers
├── Super + Space           : Fuzzel Application Launcher
├── Super + Escape          : Power Management Menu (Suspend, Poweroff)
├── Super + Shift + E       : Launch Thunar / File Manager
└── Super + Ctrl + D        : Display Topology & Resolutions (wdisplays)

Agentic & Productivity Hub
├── Super + A               : Toggle Agent Scratchpad Workspace
├── Super + N               : Open SwayNC Notification Center
├── Super + Alt + N         : Toggle Do-Not-Disturb Mode
├── Super + Alt + T         : Interactive Theme Switcher
├── Super + Ctrl + Space    : Cycle Theme Wallpapers
└── Super + K               : Open Hotkey Cheatsheet
```

---

## Conclusion

Transforming Fedora 44 into an Omarchy-inspired agentic workstation instead of simply running Arch delivers the best of both worlds: the rock-solid foundation of Red Hat's enterprise ecosystem paired with the speed and elegance of a bespoke Wayland compositor.

By shifting my mindset from simply jumping on the hype train of installing Omarchy, I chose to intentionally rice my existing setup, the journey was demanding but immensely rewarding. The desktop has become a natural extension of my developer mind—predictable, silent, and effortlessly fast.

In my next iteration, I will explore local Whisper-based voice dictation pipelines (`Phema`) wired directly into global compositor push-to-talk hotkeys, removing the keyboard barrier entirely for high-speed documentation and prompt formulation.
